content:
When I arrived at the folk-jazz-rock-fusion South Korean band Sangjaru’s Sept. 20 show at the Cedar Cultural Center, I was angry. I wasn’t the only one. I know this even though I didn’t really talk to anyone in the audience, because this was Minneapolis, in America, in 2026, and everyone there was a sentient human being. I know that we came to that concert angry, and we came tired, and then we discovered halfway through that we hadn’t actually come to a concert at all, but an exorcism. A ritual. A purification, by way of artistry and electricity and noise, noise, noise.

This isn’t to say that the part that came before the exorcism was unexceptional — far from it. Sangjaru, normally a three-piece, was for that night a duo: their guitar player, Cho Sungyoon, had been unable to travel to the United States because of visa problems. For most bands, a show sans guitarist would work about as well as a car without tires, but Sangjaru is not most bands. Between the keening, wind-torn vocalizations of Nam Seonghun’s ajaeng, a traditional Korean instrument related to the zither, and Kwon Hyochang’s ecstatically loose conjurings of dense sound from the double-helix-shaped janggu drum, there was barely space left for the prerecorded guitar. During the first few songs, I watched a man in the front row bob his head and pretend to drum along, swept up in the cloud of noise that danced on the edge of sonic overwhelm. All of this made me forget about the thing I had come to the Cedar Cultural Center so angry about. Or, at least, I was effectively distracted.

Then came the ritual. About thirty minutes in, Kwon and Nam stopped to don huge, fluffy domed hats. Kwon held up a flat brass gong and explained that this was the kkwaenggwari, the thunder-bringer, used to chase away ghosts. Tonight, he promised us, Sangjaru was going to chase all the ghosts out of Minneapolis. There was applause in response to this, but it sounded more like an exhale, or a prayer. 

All the ghosts. The wounds — not scars, because “scar” means closed, but wounds, because these cuts never will close — of people pulled from their homes, streets, schools, cars and grocery stores. I have no right to speak about what Twin Cities natives were thinking and feeling in that moment, but I know what I felt. My half-forgotten anger came back to me in a rush, now tinged with relief, release and trust. Sangjaru was going to try to fight the ghosts off, and I believed that they could do it, because I needed to believe in something. Because if you’re going to try to confront evil, hold it up in front of you by the scruff of its neck and tell it to leave you and the people you love the fuck alone. What better way to do so than music? What better way to do so than this music?

I experienced the ritual in fragments. The stage bathed in red light, the two musicians a study in contrasts: Nam standing ramrod straight behind the ajaeng, occasionally pulling a trumpet out of the air to play a gruelingly repetitive riff without breaking a sweat; Kwon a tornado of casual intensity, all solid stomps and blurrily passionate drumming. The dark bow of the ajaeng easing across the strings and into the light, all the instrument’s grace and dignity encapsulated in that simple motion. Kwon telling us to repeat after him, which we dutifully did until his voice reached heights none of us could match, heights of pitch and feeling that made the walls shake. It was too beautiful to be called violence, yet too rattling to be called anything but a confrontation. 

I came to the Sangjaru concert on Sept. 20 angry, but when I stumbled out of the Cedar Cultural Center, I felt something different. I couldn’t put it into words then, nor can I now. All I can tell you is that I wasn’t the only one who left the concert dizzy, briefly free of demons, thinking “So this is what music can do.”
